# Methods Vault

**Your personal research workspace in VS Code**

A pre-configured course workspace that organizes your journals, literature notes, project files, and textbook chapters in one place, version-controlled with Git and GitHub.

[Use this template on GitHub](https://github.com/AURA-Lab-SIUE/v2v-methods-vault){.btn .btn-primary .btn-lg}
:::

---

## What's inside

The Methods Vault is a GitHub template repository configured for this course. When you create your copy and open it in VS Code, you get a ready-to-use folder structure:

```
v2v-methods-vault/
├── 00_START_HERE.md         # Your first stop: setup instructions
├── 00_Inbox/                # Quick capture for unprocessed notes
├── 01_Journal/              # Weekly reading reflections (committed to GitHub)
├── 02_Literature/           # Reading notes and Zotero annotations
├── 03_Project/              # Your research project hub
│   ├── 01_Prospectus/       # Research design (Week 6)
│   ├── 02_Codebook/         # Data dictionary (Week 9)
│   ├── 03_Data/             # Sampled fixtures and analysis (Weeks 10 to 13)
│   └── 04_Drafts/           # Report drafts and final portfolio (Weeks 15 to 17)
├── 04_Resources/            # PDFs, images, and attachments
├── 05_Textbook/             # Chapter links for offline reading
├── _templates/              # Reusable templates for journals and data dictionaries
└── .vscode/                 # Recommended extensions, workspace settings
```

The notes are plain Markdown, so they are readable anywhere and yours forever. The workspace adds **[Foam](https://foambubble.github.io/foam/)**, a free VS Code extension that gives you `[[wiki-links]]`, a backlinks panel, and a graph view, so your journals, literature notes, and project files become a connected research archive rather than a pile of loose files.

---

## Setup guide

### Step 1: Create your copy from the template

On the [v2v-methods-vault repository](https://github.com/AURA-Lab-SIUE/v2v-methods-vault), click **Use this template**, then **Create a new repository**. Name it something like `mc451-methods-vault` and keep it private if you prefer.

### Step 2: Clone it into VS Code

In VS Code, open the Command Palette (`Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P`), run **Git: Clone**, paste your new repository URL, and choose a location you will remember (for example, `Documents/MC451/`). VS Code will offer to open the folder.

### Step 3: Install the recommended extensions

When VS Code opens the workspace, it will prompt you to install the **recommended extensions** (Foam, Quarto, the R extension, and Markdown support). Click **Install**. These are listed in `.vscode/extensions.json`, so everyone in the course works in the same environment.

### Step 4: Read the start guide

Open `00_START_HERE.md`. It walks you through the folder structure, how to start a journal entry from the template, and how Foam linking works.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Why GitHub?

Committing your workspace to GitHub gives you a backup, a history of your work, and a way for Dr. Leith to see your journal entries. It also builds the version-control habit you will use again in the final portfolio.
:::

---

## How it connects to the course

| Tool | Role | Relationship to the Vault |
|------|------|---------------------------|
| **Methods Vault** (VS Code) | Think, plan, reflect | Your primary writing workspace |
| **`v2v` R package** | Access course data | Loads the sampled fixtures you analyze, then reflect on in your journal |
| **R Workbook** | Learn R skills | Work through the [workbook labs](workbook/index.qmd) directly in VS Code |
| **Textbook** | Conceptual foundations | Linked in `05_Textbook/`; read online or alongside your workspace |

---

## Weekly workflow

1. **Start of week:** Open your Methods Vault in VS Code and pull the latest from GitHub.
2. **During the week:** Work through the week's [workbook lab](workbook/index.qmd) and read the textbook chapter.
3. **Before class:** Copy `_templates/journal-entry.md` into `01_Journal/`, rename it for the week, and write your reflection. Use `[[wiki-links]]` to connect it to your literature and project notes.
4. **After class:** Commit and push your workspace to GitHub.
